sections.title: Logline and one-page synopsis
sections.html:
1. Logline and one-page synopsis

Logline

After years supporting his mother in Las Vegas, a gifted 6'8" basketball hopeful follows his Knicks dream to New York—then jeopardizes seven artists’ trust by turning their private lives into his inspirational publicity. To earn a professional chance, he must stop measuring love by sacrifice and rebuild the support he has mistaken for an audience.

Synopsis

In darkness, a basketball meets a kick drum. Isaiah “Zay” Reed, twenty-six and 6'8", makes gravity look like a game. Seven artists join him in distinct pools of light. Almost-triumph snaps into a cramped Las Vegas kitchen: his mother, Denise, demands money and humiliates his ambition. He leaves with a ball and a small bag.

Denise is a cabaret server whose alcohol addiction has damaged work, money, and relationships. Her boyfriends were always “Uncle.” Ray Walker was the one who stayed in Zay’s life after marrying and divorcing her. Unable to remain her partner, he kept coaching the boy he believed in. At eighteen, just after graduation and as a college basketball scholarship became possible, Zay’s absent biological father died. Papers revealed that his father had submitted grant applications for him. Grief, the divorce, and fear of leaving Denise without support made Zay turn down the college route and available aid. He worked, trained with Ray, and saved for eight years.

Now his New York flight is paid for; somewhere to sleep is not settled. Ray drives him to the airport without promising a rescue. The next evening Zay finds childhood Las Vegas friend Dani at The Switch, a New York bar and cabaret. There he meets Lena, a ballet-trained exotic dancer. An intimate duet breaks when he says she could be a “real dancer again.” She orders him out. Someone whose ambition was devalued has devalued another person’s work.

Dani and roommate Ben offer three nights, then negotiate a paid arrangement. Ray provides training records and a coach introduction. Coach Simone Vale prepares Zay for a September Westchester Knicks local tryout. He earns no camp invitation. She helps him examine the film and pursue the fictional Lake Erie Forge’s November 15 application and December Buffalo camp. The Knicks remain the dream; the daily work is defense, passing, conditioning, shifts, and receiving correction.

The others pursue independent ambitions. Ben’s gallery job connects Iris to a court-side mural commission; she paints Zay without his heroic pose. Lena and Morgan develop a paid movement-and-music premiere. Velvet hires lead guitarist Jude, whose solos compete with the act. Dani betrays Ben’s confidence for a laugh. Morgan lands a film-scoring offer while avoiding a credit dispute with Jude.

A sponsor offers camp travel in exchange for Rise of Reed. Zay approves private rehearsal footage, Iris’s unfinished portrait, Dani’s harmful joke, and other people’s disclosures as evidence of his inspirational journey. Morgan licenses a rough collaborative cue without permission. Attention arrives; trust fractures. Act I leaves Zay enormous on a screen and alone beneath it.

Repair costs publicity, money, and time. Zay withdraws the film and loses the sponsor. Morgan returns the fee and negotiates proper credit. Dani apologizes without a punchline and rewrites the audition. Iris insists on an honest image license. Velvet refuses a lucrative caricature booking. Ben obtains clear acting terms. Lena requires correction before inviting Zay into a limited role in her piece. Ray helps review possessions, but will not refill Zay’s budget or make Denise’s recovery his responsibility.

A December 14 camp callback conflicts with the premiere. Zay discloses it, pays for rehearsed cover, and asks for release. The show proceeds without him. At camp, he accepts correction and makes the extra pass. Days later comes a six-week paid Forge contract—a first professional step, with the NBA still far away. The others gain work and firmer boundaries at different speeds. Denise remains responsible for her own recovery. Zay can love her without moving back. In the finale, he leaves space between impacts. Eight distinct colors hold; someone else can carry the beat.

sections.title: Character bible
sections.html:
2. Character bible

All principals are adults. Ages, identities, and relationship configurations are working choices for casting and development. The seven familiar chakra colors form a theatrical design vocabulary; pearl-white Soul Star is BOUNCE’s artistic eighth extension, not a claim that this eight-part scheme is a universally established traditional system. Color describes pressure and change rather than personality type or spiritual attainment.

Isaiah “Zay” Reed • 26 • professional basketball hopeful • solar plexus / yellow

Ambition and craft. Born and raised in Las Vegas, Zay has wanted to play for the New York Knicks since childhood. At 6'8", he can defend several positions and see over a trap, but he overdribbles when he feels watched. Years of warehouse and event shifts fund training, family bills, and finally a New York flight and local-tryout budget. He has continued competitive adult-league play and supervised work with Ray; his talent has not survived on wish alone. His September Westchester Knicks G League tryout does not produce a camp invitation. Vale helps him turn that disappointment into a plan for current, continuous game film and the independent Forge opportunity. Show possession labels, closeout angles, weak-side rotations, free throws while tired, and a smaller offensive role. Madison Square Garden is a destination he imagines, not the location of an open NBA audition.

Upbringing and coping. Denise, a single mother and server at Las Vegas’s fictional Desert Star cabaret, could remember a table’s entire order and save for Zay’s shoes, then drink away money they needed and make tenderness conditional on his usefulness. Each new boyfriend was introduced as “Uncle”; Zay learned to attach quickly and pack his feelings when a man disappeared. Ray Walker married Denise, then divorced her when he could no longer participate in the relationship amid her addiction. He kept his commitment to Zay: practices, film, transport, applications. Zay calls him Uncle Ray, never mistakes him for a blood relative, and mistrusts every missed call as a possible ending. He is funny about his height, playful with children, and quietly excellent at repairing household objects.

The college choice. Zay finished high school at eighteen. That summer, while a basketball scholarship route was coming together, his long-absent biological father died. Among the papers were copies of grant applications his father had submitted on his behalf, alongside an unfinished form for another fund. Applications were not awards, and the late gesture did not undo the years he was absent. A coach and aid office had made a possible college package concrete, but grief and Denise’s recent divorce from Ray convinced Zay that leaving would abandon his family. He declined the college place and available support, took more paid shifts, and stayed. The story respects that constrained choice without calling it destiny or the only responsible option. He carries anger both at the father who did not show up and at himself for the life he did not take.

Flaw. He hears correction as a verdict on his worth. He reproduces the hierarchy that hurts him: paid over unpaid, professional over amateur, respectable over embarrassing. He thinks giving people exposure is generosity even when it removes their choices.

Relationships. Dani knew him in their Las Vegas neighborhood and moved to New York earlier; Ben insists that a couch has a calendar. Lena resists becoming proof that he is a good man. Iris sees him accurately. Vale evaluates choices, not mythology. Ray is a chosen mentor with limits, not an unlimited father-shaped resource. Denise remains someone he loves and cannot safely live with; care does not require surrendering his income, location, or future.

Decisive choice and cost. He authorizes withdrawal of Rise of Reed before knowing whether anyone will help replace the lost travel money. Later he asks to be released from his performance commitment, arranges paid cover, and accepts that the answer could be no.

Progress. A six-week paid injury-cover Forge contract, with no promise of renewal or NBA affiliation. The Knicks dream stays alive without a miraculous call-up. He rents a modest room, contributes a fixed affordable amount to Denise without accepting unrestricted demands, and retains a training plan. He thanks Ray for specific help rather than asking whether Ray will stay forever. Yellow loses its brittle, overexposed edge; his body occupies space without demanding every eye.

Supporting family roles and chronology

Denise Reed — mother and Las Vegas cabaret server. A skilled, funny worker who knows regulars and protects a new server from a rude customer, she also misses shifts, lies about drinking, and humiliates her son. The profession does not cause the addiction and the addiction does not excuse the abuse. Her concrete desire is to keep her job and apartment. Her independent late-story action is making her own call about support and requesting a shift arrangement; neither sobriety nor reconciliation is certified by the finale. Zay cannot do recovery on her behalf.

Ray “Uncle Ray” Walker — former stepfather, coach, and mentor. One of the men called Uncle became a temporary father figure and did not discard Zay when the marriage ended. Ray’s early help includes practice plans, reliable rides, game-film records, and introducing Zay to Vale. He has work and obligations of his own. He refuses to mediate the old marriage, promises no roster place, and cannot keep paying emergencies. He once mistook Zay’s silence for agreement; he now asks before giving advice. His decisive act is telling Zay that choosing his own future is compatible with loving Denise, then remaining reachable after Zay actually leaves.

Biological father — absent, later deceased. He is present through papers and Zay’s conflicting memories, not a redemptive ghost. His late grant effort creates a question the son cannot ask him; it does not prove a secret lifetime of good parenting.

Timeline to protect in every version: High-school graduation at eighteen → biological father’s death as college scholarship plans mature → discovery of grant paperwork, with Denise and Ray already divorced → Zay declines college/available aid and stays to earn → eight years of paid work, family support, training, and saving → Las Vegas departure at twenty-six → New York arrival and September G League local tryout → November 15 Forge film deadline → December 12–14 camp/premiere conflict. The eight principal chakra identities remain unchanged; these family roles do not add a ninth symbolic identity.

Lena Marlow • 28 • ballet-trained dancer and working exotic dancer • sacral / orange

Ambition and craft. Lena wants a paid, self-directed movement piece. Ballet, floorwork, club dancing, balance, improvisation, and managing an audience are all in her vocabulary. She knows which shoes survive which floors, negotiates bookings, and can make a room laugh with a single held balance. She enjoys desire and attention when she has chosen their terms.

Upbringing and coping. A family proud of her discipline outsourced emotional approval to teachers and casting decisions. A training culture taught her to monitor her body as an object. When tuition assistance ended and a rent shortfall made unpaid ballet work unsustainable, a colleague introduced her to paid exotic dancing; financial urgency opened that door, while her present choices reflect skills, pleasures, and terms she has made her own. She now protects herself with competence and quick judgments about whose interest is safe.

Flaw. She sometimes assumes that asking for help means surrendering control. She may cancel a promising collaboration rather than negotiate a boundary, leaving other people to guess what she needed.

Relationships. Velvet exchanges rehearsal space and teaches her audience control; she helps Velvet find movement sustainable across a full set. Morgan is a creative partner, with choreography credit and a share of the project fee. Zay becomes a possible friend and attraction only after the bar incident is addressed.

Decisive choice and cost. She declines a better-paid booking that would give a promoter ownership of new choreography and keeps selected club shifts to finance rehearsal. She requires Morgan to amend the cue agreement and Zay to remove her footage before continuing with either.

Progress. A paid premiere, a clean recording license, and a proposal for a second engagement. She continues exotic dance by choice while developing choreography; ballet is a living resource rather than a status she must reclaim. She initiates the later invitation to Zay: coffee, no audience, no promise. Orange carries pleasure as well as injury.

Dani Price • 27 • comedian • throat / blue

Ambition and craft. Dani wants a four-week paid opening slot with a regional touring comic, beginning in January. They keep a notebook of tags, time sets, cut material that drags, and rewrite transitions after listening to recordings. Their comic eye catches the bureaucratic absurdities of city survival.

Upbringing and coping. Dani grew up reading raised voices before understanding the argument. A joke could interrupt danger. Now a laugh can feel like proof that a room is safe, even when the person being laughed at is not.

Flaw. Dani turns confidences into bits before checking whose experience is being used. Their joke about Ben knowing how to pack before anyone asks him to leave is skilled, revealing, and a betrayal. Calling it “truth” does not make it theirs to sell.

Relationships. Zay is a childhood friend from Las Vegas; Dani moved to New York before him and knows how much it cost him to buy the flight. He is not a new rescue project. Ben is roommate and rehearsal partner with an independent right to privacy. Velvet eventually hires Dani to host the headline set, with a clear fee and no personal material about the company.

Decisive choice and cost. Dani cuts the strongest laugh in the audition set, requests removal of a posted clip, and accepts that the booker must see a new tape. In silence at the apartment table, they tell Ben: “You trusted me with that. I used it. You don’t have to make me feel better.” They do not add a joke.

Progress. The paid opening engagement comes after a second audition, not from notoriety. Ben resumes rehearsing with them under explicit limits; trust is partial. Blue grows clearer when Dani stops using volume and wit to fill every pause.

Andre Bell / Velvet Saint • 30 • drag performer • crown / violet

Ambition and craft. Andre is a drag artist whose stage persona, Velvet Saint, marries live vocal authority, comic timing, costume engineering, and exact audience control. The goal is a headline show with a guaranteed fee, rehearsal pay, and approval over promotion. Andre tracks ticket sales, cues costume changes, and repairs a fastening while negotiating a contract.

Upbringing and coping. Acceptance depended on an approved public identity. Velvet is invention and pleasure, not simply armor; nevertheless Andre sometimes brings the command of the persona into private conversations where vulnerability would work better.

Flaw. Andre equates being indispensable with belonging. A tempting corporate booking offers good money for a flattened, insulting act. Taking it could finance the desired show while teaching everyone what can be bought.

Relationships. Lena is a colleague who can contradict Andre without asking permission. Jude is an employee whose talent must serve a complete theatrical event. Dani becomes a host rather than an unpaid friend filling a gap.

Decisive choice and cost. Andre declines the caricature brief after trying—and failing—to negotiate its terms. The loss means a smaller venue, a reused costume, and two fewer musical arrangements. Andre tells Lena plainly that the refusal hurts, instead of presenting it as effortless righteousness.

Progress. A modest headline run with a guaranteed minimum and a stronger live act. Andre learns to invite someone to dinner without making the invitation a performance. Violet connects separate people; it does not dissolve them into Velvet’s spotlight.

Ben Mercer • 25 • actor • root / red

Ambition and craft. Ben wants a meaningful role and enough stability to arrive prepared. He works temporary installation and event shifts, uses action verbs on scripts, records self-tapes against a borrowed wall, and listens closely when Dani gives him a line differently.

Upbringing and coping. Several unstable households taught Ben to discover the useful version of himself quickly. He is generous, observant, a good cook from whatever is left, and alarmingly able to say yes before hearing the question.

Flaw. Conflicting promises cause actual harm: he misses an installation call after covering a friend’s shift, leaving Iris to lift a panel she should not handle alone. His evasions are understandable but not harmless.

Relationships. Dani shares rent and rehearsal, then violates a confidence. Iris becomes a professional collaborator who asks him for a schedule he can honor. Zay learns from him that housing generosity requires consent from both residents.

Decisive choice and cost. Ben turns down an open-ended unpaid rehearsal request and asks for dates, a fee, and replacement terms. He risks being called difficult. He also admits an earlier missed call directly to Iris and completes paid repair work on an agreed schedule.

Progress. A small, paid role in a three-week new-play engagement, plus a predictable installation contract. He keeps his apartment share rather than abandoning it for a vague promise. Red becomes a place to stand rather than an alarm.

Jude Reyes • 29 • musician specializing in lead guitar • heart / green

Ambition and craft. Jude wants steady paid work and a sound recognizably his own. His vocabulary includes rock attack, funk restraint, and a singing, slightly delayed melodic turn. He understands tone, touring gear, and how to finish a difficult run; he is learning how to stop before the run.

Upbringing and coping. Inconsistent affection made emotional exposure feel like an invitation to withdrawal. Mastery offers a controlled form of intimacy. Jude cooks for people and leaves before they can thank him.

Flaw. Competition turns a collaborative cue into a solo opportunity. He claims that the music “speaks for itself,” conveniently avoiding a credit conversation until resentment has already entered the work.

Relationships. Morgan composes structure, harmony, and dramatic timing; Jude contributes a lead part and, where genuinely co-written, a melodic theme. Velvet can fire him for ignoring a cue. Lena helps him hear what a dancer needs between counts.

Decisive choice and cost. Jude agrees to a shorter featured solo and a documented division of composition and performance credit. He tells Morgan which phrase was his and which was not, and stays for the uncomfortable discussion instead of unplugging.

Progress. A paid live residency with Velvet and a sustainable scoring collaboration with Morgan. No label deal appears. Green moves from a virtuoso phrase held apart from the band to a phrase that answers another voice.

Iris Chen • 31 • painter • third eye / indigo

Ambition and craft. Iris wants a paid mural commission and a small exhibition that represent her own eye. She studies underpainting, tests pigments under the actual center lights, documents wall preparation, and separates a proposal image from a licensed finished work. Her dry humor is precise enough to feel like a small incision.

Upbringing and coping. Her household prized the appearance of calm over admitting what happened. She learned to make pleasing images and doubt uncomfortable perceptions. Now she can diagnose another person’s defenses while showing almost nothing of herself.

Flaw. She calls withholding “observation.” A portrait sitting with Zay risks becoming another extraction until she tells him what she sees, asks what he wishes to protect, and permits him to refuse a pose.

Relationships. Ben connects her to the center and becomes a collaborator whose labor she must value. Zay is a paid sitter within her commission budget, not free inspirational material. Morgan asks to project the portrait and must obtain permission like anyone else.

Decisive choice and cost. Iris rejects a sponsor’s request to remove the tired, unguarded hands from Zay’s image. She accepts a smaller approved production budget and negotiates a separate reproduction license. She also includes one small self-portrait in her gallery proposal, exposing her own unfinishedness.

Progress. The mural is paid in installments, with the final payment after installation acceptance. A two-person exhibition opens later; several paintings remain unsold. Indigo reveals surfaces and layers without giving Iris supernatural insight.

Morgan Ellis • 28 • songwriter, composer, and scorer • Soul Star / pearl white

Ambition and craft. Morgan wants properly credited composition work in film and theater. Songwriting means character, lyric, and melody; composing means form and harmonic architecture; scoring means meeting a picture’s timing and emotional need. Morgan can hear how fragments fit, but is also capable of writing a spare cue that belongs only to Morgan.

Upbringing and coping. A parent’s unrealized musical ambitions turned Morgan’s achievements into family compensation. Managing other people’s feelings became a practical skill. Morgan is funny about sound, meticulous with pencils, and secretly fond of a very unfashionable cadence.

Flaw. Morgan volunteers other people’s work as readily as their own time, mistaking collaboration for permission. Licensing the rough promo cue without clearing Jude’s recorded performance and Lena’s choreography is a consequential breach, even though Zay approves the film’s final cut.

Relationships. Jude challenges ownership and listening. Lena insists that movement has authorship. A short-film director offers an independent score with a real deadline; Morgan jeopardizes it by hiding delays while servicing everyone else.

Decisive choice and cost. Morgan withdraws the rough cue, returns the license fee, and names each contributor. They tell the film director the actual schedule, negotiate one fewer revision round, and risk losing the job instead of delivering an apology disguised as endless free work.

Progress. A completed, paid short-film score credited as “Original score by Morgan Ellis,” with Jude’s separately agreed credit for a co-written theme and guitar performance where applicable. The stage piece credits Lena’s choreography and shared concept explicitly. Pearl white makes room for the other colors without washing them away.

sections.title: Relationship map
sections.html:
3. Relationship map

The opening is a symbolic assembly across distance. At the start of the literal story, Zay is still in Las Vegas and knows Dani from their childhood neighborhood; Dani is already in New York; Dani lives with Ben; Lena and Velvet are colleagues; Jude and Morgan already collaborate. Other connections are made onstage through an introduction, a job, or a negotiation.

Connection Why they meet Choice that changes the other person’s path
Zay ↔ Dani Childhood Las Vegas neighborhood friendship; Dani now works in New York, including a booking at The Switch Dani offers bounded emergency shelter. Zay later refuses to let the promo’s removal wait for Dani’s career calculation, forcing an honest decision about the clip.
Dani ↔ Ben Shared apartment and reciprocal audition practice Dani’s joke endangers trust and the apartment’s safety. Ben stops serving as automatic rehearsal partner; Dani must write and audition again.
Ben ↔ Iris Ben installs work at Iris’s gallery Ben introduces Iris to a center administrator he knows through event shifts. Iris later hires him on clear installation terms that support his acting schedule.
Iris ↔ Zay Recreation-center mural beside the court Iris insists on a seated portrait showing hands and breath. Zay’s later consent to the honest finished image changes the mural and his public self-presentation.
Lena ↔ Velvet Different nights at The Switch; shared studio rental Lena reshapes a movement transition so Velvet can sing live without injury. Velvet offers Lena a paid rehearsal slot and insists on a written choreography license.
Velvet ↔ Jude Velvet hires a live guitarist Velvet stops a run and threatens to replace Jude if he ignores vocal cues. Jude’s revised arrangement makes the live headline act viable with a smaller band.
Jude ↔ Morgan Existing music collaboration Jude demands specificity about a melody he contributed. Morgan creates a written credit split; Jude’s willingness to serve the cue helps Morgan deliver the independent film score.
Morgan ↔ Lena Joint proposal for the center’s movement-and-music commission Morgan’s unauthorized cue license breaks the project. Lena’s refusal to proceed until it is corrected teaches Morgan that integration is not ownership.
Lena ↔ Zay Bar conversation, then later center work Lena ends the first encounter. Only after repair does she invite Zay to contribute a basketball phrase; she also insists that another performer learn it.
Ben ↔ Zay Temporary housing and premiere logistics Ben asks for rent dates and exit terms. Zay later pays a substitute mover rather than using Ben’s habit of saying yes to solve his camp conflict.
Dani ↔ Velvet Comedy introduction through Lena Velvet pays Dani to host a smaller headline engagement after seeing a revised set; Dani’s reliable hosting gives Velvet room to change costumes and breathe.
Iris ↔ Morgan Requests to use images in the premiere and promo Iris’s image license forces Morgan to separate visual permission from musical permission. Morgan later budgets and credits the approved projection.

Family connections that remain active across distance: Denise’s demands helped make Zay the family earner and delayed college; his decision to leave forces both to confront the limits of that arrangement. Ray’s coaching, records, and introduction to Vale create a route to evaluation without buying the result. Ray’s refusal to act as go-between with Denise changes Zay’s habit of managing every adult. The biological father’s papers complicate grief without replacing present-day relationships. These supporting ties sit around the eight-person network, not above it.

Network consequence: Removal of the promo stops a common source of visibility, but it does not require a collective verdict. Velvet supports withdrawal immediately; Dani initially fears losing the booking; Iris demands removal of the image; Lena pauses rehearsal; Jude removes his recorded part; Morgan acknowledges the unauthorized license; Ben refuses to mediate the argument for everyone. Each can make a different choice without being reduced to a vote on Zay.

sections.title: Two-act Broadway treatment
sections.html:
4. Two-act Broadway treatment

Working running time: Approximately 135 minutes including a fifteen-minute interval. A live band of keys, bass, drums/percussion, and guitar can expand with reeds or strings as resources allow. Jude’s featured playing must be credible; a visible instrumental double may support demanding passages without pretending the actor performs unavailable technique.

Stage grammar: One sprung central floor holds a court arc, a studio, and the open area of an apartment. Tracked frames and practical lamps create rooms without turning every location into a projection. The Switch is one workplace among several. Bench, barre, easel, folding table, guitar rig, and a door have specific dramatic jobs. No color substitutes for an action.

Act I • August to early November • the price of being seen

Opening / “BOUNCE.” A symbolic six-minute assembly gives each person pleasure and skill before biography. Zay establishes the groove alone. His routes remain clear as the others appear, and he catches the ball for demanding vocal phrases. Their individual desires overlap into an almost-resolved chorus. The kick stops. Denise’s exact household confrontation collapses the fantasy into a cramped Las Vegas kitchen. Her Desert Star server’s apron, a real overdue bill, and a concealed drink make the pressures specific. Zay leaves without a comeback speech, taking the small bag packed for a flight he has saved for and already booked.

The journey and The Switch / “AFTER THE APPLAUSE.” Keys, door, shoes, Las Vegas traffic, a brief call with Ray, an airport announcement, and a New York train carry one continuous rhythmic transition. Ray drives Zay to the red-eye but cannot give him a future on credit. A clear place-and-time shift makes the next evening’s arrival in New York literal. The Switch is not Denise’s workplace. Dani, who left their Las Vegas neighborhood earlier, is working. Lena initiates a conversation about Zay’s restless footwork, and a duet finds common ground in being watched. Zay’s “real dancer again” remark breaks it. She gives him a chance to explain, then orders him out. He obeys. The band does not sentimentalize his exit.

Three nights / “TERMS AND CONDITIONS.” In Dani and Ben’s apartment, a fitted sheet becomes a temporary sleeping place. Ben says “Of course” to a new guest before realizing what the week already contains. Dani stops the automatic agreement. They negotiate three nights, quiet hours, a key, and a check-in. Comedy comes from space: Zay’s feet occupy the route to the kettle. The number becomes a calendar of shifts, auditions, rent, and gym hours. Ben teaches Zay a load-in pattern of carrying, setting, and releasing weight; it later becomes transferable percussion.

A role, not a rescue. Ray sends continuous Las Vegas game film and introduces Zay to Coach Vale; she does not owe Ray a favorable answer. At the recreation center she watches Zay dominate a casual run, then lose a defensive assignment. She prepares him for a September Westchester local tryout. He storms out after “You were late on the rotation,” then returns the following morning and asks to see the possession again. At the tryout, gifted players expose the cost of his overdribbling. No camp invitation follows. Vale helps him build toward the independent Forge’s November 15 film deadline instead. This is a new plan, not a claim that the Forge feeds the Knicks. The return to work is small and imperfect. Meanwhile Ben’s gallery call introduces Iris to the administrator selecting the mural artist. Iris submits samples, a budget, and a schedule; the commission is not awarded as a favor.

The folder. After the tryout rejection, Zay empties his bag looking for an old stat sheet and finds copies of the college papers he kept. Dani recognizes the year. At the kitchen table he puts the scholarship correspondence beside his father’s unfinished grant form: “He found the office. Couldn’t find my gym.” Dani does not turn it into a joke or tell him the papers prove love. On a call, Ray acknowledges that he was moving out just as Zay needed adults to stay. “I thought staying home meant I was the man,” Zay says. Ray answers, “You were eighteen.” Zay folds the papers away and asks for the next practice time. The scene identifies grief and a sacrificed opportunity without treating his talent as untouched by the intervening years.

Movement and ownership / “WEIGHT OF MY OWN.” In a hired rehearsal room, Lena makes a ballet preparation change direction into her own floorwork. Morgan tries to label the movement with a melody before listening to it. Lena stops: “That’s where I breathe.” The song becomes a negotiated collaboration. They draft the center proposal with separate fees for choreography and composition, a rehearsal budget, and a contingency performer. Zay is not in the scene.

The headline act / “A ROOM THAT HOLDS.” Velvet, Jude, and Lena work in the studio before a drag night. Jude’s spectacular flourish conceals a missed cue. Velvet stops the band and has him play underneath a held word until he understands the audience’s attention. A promoter later offers a much larger fee for an insulting, tightly controlled caricature. Andre says they will consider the offer; money has a legitimate pull.

The portrait / “WHAT THE LIGHT KEEPS.” Iris sketches Zay at the center. He asks to stand with the ball above his head. She asks him to sit and let his hands rest. He resists; she admits that her first proposal painted over everything difficult. Their duet makes looking reciprocal. Nearby, Vale conducts film study: the next pass exists before the defender makes it obvious. Zay begins to understand the same idea in two languages.

The joke and the missed call. Dani tries new material in a small comedy room and gets a huge laugh from Ben’s private history. Ben hears a recording later at home. His anger is not a theatrical walkout; he stops helping with the self-tape and asks for the clip to come down. Separately, Ben misses Iris’s scheduled installation because he said yes to another shift. Iris’s anger gives him no morally superior place to hide. Both scenes require an answer without music.

Credit / “COUNTERMELODY.” In Morgan’s workroom, Jude and Morgan build a cue. A four-note guitar phrase becomes the piece’s emotional center. Neither names the ownership question directly. Morgan receives a paid short-film scoring offer but conceals its deadline to avoid disappointing Lena. Zay arrives with an offer from a local sponsor: travel and camp lodging in exchange for a public profile film. Morgan agrees to supply a rough cue. “We made it together” is treated as sufficient permission when it is not.

The film / “IN THE FRAME.” Over several rehearsals, Zay gives the filmmaker material labeled for private rehearsal review and approves a cut that converts his friends into adversity around him. A vulnerable Lena voice memo about controlling her own movement is placed under club footage; Ben’s history is carried by Dani’s joke; Iris’s unfinished portrait is cropped into an emblem of heroic strength. Morgan licenses the cue before obtaining the necessary clearances. The film’s attractive presentation matters: Zay can see the version of himself he desperately wants to believe. Its “son who saved his family” framing flatters his sacrifice and erases Ray’s work. Zay agrees to that simplification before applying the same extraction to his friends. The film must not present addiction or Lena’s occupation as decorative evidence of his heroism without the drama exposing the harm.

At the center, a small screening coincides with the film’s public release. Early congratulatory notifications become objections in the room. Each principal sings a version of “That isn’t what I gave you.” Zay answers with “People are finally looking,” revealing the mistake rather than resolving it. The ensemble’s phrases compete, and the ball finds no place in the groove. A large projected face remains above eight separated bodies. Act I turning point: success as exposure has cost the support that made it possible.

Act II • November to December • the work after the promise

The morning after / “LOOK AGAIN.” Seven separate spaces, no tribunal. Lena cancels the next joint rehearsal. Iris writes a removal request. Jude mutes the guitar stem. Velvet calls the sponsor to reject use of the act. Dani calculates whether the new booking inquiry will vanish; Ben tells them calculation is not an apology. Morgan opens the cue agreement and sees exactly what they authorized. Zay first tries to explain intention, then reads the materials he ignored. He orders removal and posts a correction naming the affected work and its owners. A copy cannot be guaranteed to disappear from every account; he continues requests without claiming the harm has been erased.

Practical cost. The sponsor withdraws camp funding under the proposed agreement; Zay does not sue his way out of a dramatic choice. He sells a nonessential item, accepts additional stockroom shifts, and takes paid assistant hours in the center’s youth program under Vale’s supervision. He misses one optional training slot and adjusts the plan rather than pretending exhaustion is heroic. He submits continuous game film by November 15, with no inspirational edit. Ray helps label possessions but declines a request to cover the lost sponsor money. They keep the next film-review appointment anyway: a limit is not abandonment.

The plain sentence / “NO PUNCHLINE.” Dani rehearses a confession that keeps turning into a bit. The music stops before the actual apartment conversation. They acknowledge using Ben and do not request immediate forgiveness. The replacement audition set exposes Dani’s own need to control a room. Ben will not laugh on cue; later, an unforced laugh returns over a separate small absurdity while they cook.

Authorship / “PUT MY NAME ON IT.” Morgan returns the promo fee and renegotiates with the short-film director. Jude and Morgan distinguish the score, the co-written theme, the arrangement, and the recorded guitar part. The work becomes more intimate because it becomes clearer. Jude plays the melody once, without embellishment. Morgan lets their own vocal line finish. A fee schedule and a realistic revision limit are part of the scene’s liberation.

A new invitation / “HOLD FOR EIGHT.” Lena hears Zay’s apology in a neutral hallway, before rehearsal: he judged her livelihood, then used her image; both were choices. He does not ask to enter the studio. Days later she invites him to contribute a footwork phrase to the center piece, with a defined fee and permission limited to that project. She builds a version any trained cast member can carry. Velvet declines the large caricature booking after the promoter refuses changes; the smaller show proceeds with fewer costumes and a stronger arrangement. Lena and Velvet celebrate a workable phrase, not moral purity.

Receiving the pass / “SECOND READ.” On court, Vale corrects Zay in front of other players. His old response starts in his shoulders. This time he asks, “Show me where you needed me.” He repeats the defensive rotation, then makes the pass that begins someone else’s successful possession. He receives the December camp invitation. Back in his New York room, Denise calls from Las Vegas about an overdue bill. He offers an amount he can actually pay and ends the call when she starts humiliating him. Ray will not carry messages between them. In a separate brief Vegas scene, Denise irons her server’s shirt, acknowledges a missed shift to her manager, and makes her own call about support. The action is hers; the production does not announce a recovery she has not yet lived. Neither love nor the unpaid balance disappears.

Boundaries that hold / “THE WORK OF STAYING.” Ben negotiates his first small paid acting engagement. It conflicts with an installation call; he tells Iris early and helps identify a qualified replacement rather than secretly attempting both. Iris accepts the solution and pays the contracted hours. Dani receives the January opening engagement on the strength of the revised tape. These gains occur before the climax so the ending need not distribute prizes to everyone at once.

The extension. The camp was scheduled for December 12–13 with a possible December 14 callback disclosed in the invitation. Zay has held travel funds for the possibility but hoped not to need it. After the first day he is asked to remain. The center premiere is December 14; he had promised load-in labor and a short live ball part. He calls before rehearsal ends. Lena will not cancel the show or absorb unpaid labor. Zay activates the contingency rehearsed earlier, transfers his performer fee to the substitute, pays a replacement mover, and accepts that Lena is disappointed. Ben verifies the handoff without giving up his own acting call. Friendship functions through planning and consent.

Climax / “ENOUGH FOR TONIGHT.” Two places coexist onstage. At camp, Zay is tired and trying to earn trust against players with equal need. At the center, a lighting cue fails; Lena holds an intentional count, Morgan picks up the next entrance, and the piece continues. The mural is revealed as part of a building in use, not as Zay’s shrine. In the scrimmage, Zay can take a difficult shot or pass to a better-positioned teammate. He passes, then recovers on defense. The coach records something; no contract descends from the rafters. The premiere ends with applause, then the company stacks chairs and checks the settlement sheet.

Epilogue / “BOUNCE (LEAVE SOME ROOM).” Days and weeks move in practical details. Zay receives the six-week paid offer and reads its dates with Vale. He calls Ray to discuss the actual role, then thanks him for getting up before dawn for years. Ray asks when the next practice is; he does not demand a father’s title or credit for the contract. Morgan delivers the score. Velvet’s smaller run meets its guarantee. Iris signs off the final mural payment and hangs an unsold painting. Ben arrives early to rehearsal. Dani packs for January. Lena begins a second-project budget and invites Zay for coffee before he leaves. Denise and Zay speak briefly across the country; he does not promise to move home or cure her drinking. A boundary remains in place. His worn Knicks cap is still in the bag beside the Forge paperwork: the dream has acquired a next step, not an ending. The ball returns, and each principal can hold the pulse while Zay listens. Final turning point: no one must become a supporting character in someone else’s proof of worth.

sections.title: Three-act feature-film adaptation
sections.html:
5. Three-act feature-film adaptation

Working length: Approximately 118–125 minutes. Preserve the musical form: songs remain discoveries and actions, not background montages replacing scenes. Maintain Zay’s emotional viewpoint while permitting substantial sequences where he is absent.

Film Act I • approximately minutes 0–32 • the city and the closed door

The opening begins on a ball descending into darkness. Match its impact to a real court and an exact kick. Zay owns the first uninterrupted passage: full-body movement, a grin, a difficult change of direction. Each new character is introduced in a separate physical location—a self-tape wall, empty studio, comedy mic check, dressing room, rehearsal booth, paint worktable, and composition desk. Match foot pivots, pencil taps, guitar fingering, and rehearsal counts. Do not cut between interchangeable close-ups so rapidly that skill disappears.

The chorus permits impossible spatial connections without suggesting these people are literally together. As the opening reaches resolution, cut hard to the fixed, cramped Las Vegas kitchen frame. Denise’s exact line arrives without a score. Hold Zay’s body in that frame long enough for his familiar stillness to register. On leaving, stay at his height initially, then let the camera remain inside while he bends through the door: the departure has cost.

The journey to The Switch has geography and elapsed time: Las Vegas service entrances and traffic, Ray’s car before the airport, the prepaid red-eye, a New York arrival board, and finally an evening train. A brief shot of the boarding pass and Zay’s remaining budget makes the saved fare legible; a deleted message to Dani makes the unsolved housing legible. Preserve keys, latch, and footsteps as the musical seed. Ray’s goodbye is practical—charger, film link, practice time—not a speech about destiny. At the bar, let Lena move and initiate. Their duet uses patient shared frames and small changes of distance. When he says “real dancer,” resist cutting immediately to an explanatory flashback. Her face and his attempt to explain are enough. He leaves when told.

Compress the apartment negotiations and early job search into a short sequence, but retain Ben’s consent and Coach Vale’s first correction as full scenes. Establish that Ray arranged the introduction, not the outcome. Act I break: Zay returns to the court after walking out and commits to preparing for the September Westchester local tryout. He has reached New York; he has not reached the NBA.

Film Act II • approximately minutes 32–91 • who owns the image

Begin with the local tryout and the absence of a camp invitation: show Zay checking the actual result, then reviewing the possessions he wanted to avoid. The Forge deadline becomes his next practical route. Keep the grant-folder scene as a present-day conversation with Dani and a call to Ray; use only brief, motivated inserts of his high-school graduation and dated applications, not a sentimental biography montage. His father’s death and his choice to stay must remain separate from a claim that the scholarship itself vanished.

Use the city to give the independent lives texture: Ben on a gallery ladder and then at an audition; Iris testing color on the center wall; Lena checking her pay at work and inventing movement in daylight; Andre negotiating a contract on a costume shop stair; Jude loading an amplifier onto a train; Morgan spotting a film cue against a timecode. These are lived tasks rather than picturesque hardship.

“WEIGHT OF MY OWN,” “A ROOM THAT HOLDS,” and “WHAT THE LIGHT KEEPS” retain enough continuous performance to show craft. “TERMS AND CONDITIONS” can recur instrumentally under calendars, travel, and room changes. Dani’s harmful joke is filmed from the back of a small room, then heard again through a phone in the apartment, where its emotional scale changes. Jude and Morgan’s credit argument stays in one workroom: cinematic intimacy need not mean cutting away.

Move the sponsor offer earlier than in the stage treatment so the film’s central temptation has time to seduce. Show Zay reviewing the actual promo cut with visible permission notes beside the assets. He sees the objectionable material and clicks approval; no editor secretly creates his moral mistake. Morgan’s cue decision is a separate scene and responsibility.

Midpoint, around minute 62: Rise of Reed appears publicly. Screen fragments through devices in different workplaces before bringing several principals together for the center rehearsal. Zay experiences praise while Lena experiences recognition without consent. “IN THE FRAME” becomes the counterpoint between a polished public narrative and eight people being rearranged by it.

The back half of Act II gives removal, corrections, returned money, damaged bookings, revised tape, and real rehearsals time to occur. Zay’s specific apology to Lena receives its own scene; her later invitation is another scene on another day. A short return to Denise’s Las Vegas workplace permits her skill, damaged employment, and effort to seek support to exist outside Zay’s point of view. A call with Ray stays on Zay when Ray says he cannot lend more money; later, the still-kept coaching appointment disproves the abandonment Zay expects. The film score deadline gives Morgan a separate clock. The independent opportunities advance before the basketball climax. Act II break: Zay reaches Buffalo and earns the camp extension, then must call New York and make the handoff he once would have assumed people owed him.

Film Act III • approximately minutes 91–122 • leave room

Intercut the December 14 scrimmage and premiere through decisions rather than a fantasy of one shared live event. There is no video call cheering Zay from the stage and no improbable trip between cities. Keep the ball acoustically dry in the gym; let the score enter the film’s expressive space only after the physical rhythm is established. Lena’s count, Morgan’s cue, and Zay’s breath can rhyme without suggesting telepathy.

Shoot the extra pass wide enough to show the defense and its consequence. The important athletic proof is the read and next defensive recovery, not a slow-motion winning shot. At the premiere, preserve an uncut section of Lena’s choreography and the other performer carrying Zay’s phrase. The company has acquired a method, not a mascot.

After the show, stay for chair stacking, fee envelopes or transfers, sore feet, and an ordinary laugh. After camp, show the ride back without a decision. The offer arrives several days later in a quiet room. Zay reads rather than screams; six weeks is concrete and limited. He shares the dates with Ray, and a separate short call with Denise maintains the financial boundary. No cut to Madison Square Garden suggests an NBA contract that has not been earned. In the closing reprise, return to the opening locations with altered behavior: Dani lets silence remain, Jude listens, Morgan’s name appears on an actual credit, Lena chooses the next move. A final real court gathering can unite the eight after the chronology has earned it. Eight colors enter through separate practical sources and costume details; no rainbow filter flattens the city.

Meaningful adaptation changes: The stage uses a single floor, an announced overnight journey, and live rhythmic handoffs to make interdependence visible. The film can distinguish Las Vegas service corridors from New York rehearsal spaces, show the red-eye’s elapsed time, and revisit Denise and Ray without teleporting them into the ensemble. It uses distance, transit time, screens, and editing to reveal how publicity travels faster than consent and repair. The stage ends Act I at the promotional fracture; the film places that event at its midpoint. Film gives more room to private labor and waiting, while preserving the exact opening shock, household confrontation, bar exchange, and accountability spine.

sections.title: Working score • sixteen numbers
sections.html:
6. Working score • sixteen numbers

Shared musical DNA: The opening lives at 96 BPM in 4/4. Its principal rhythmic cell is two grounded attacks, a rest, then a quicker return; real ball impacts anchor the attacks while the band maintains time. A rising fourth followed by a step down becomes the question behind “what am I worth?” Motifs can share intervals without every character singing the same tune. Gospel-rooted ensemble harmony provides communal answering, soul and R&B supply conversational elasticity, funk supports work and footwork, guitar brings attack and tenderness, and jazz-inflected voicings make room for uncertainty. These are original compositional directions, not requests to imitate a particular artist.

# Working title / singers Dramatic action and musical character Reprise plan
1 BOUNCE — Zay, then all eight Six-minute opening. Ball and kick establish a 96 BPM groove; bass, percussion, harmony, guitar, and keys enter in layers. Each principal gets an audible want before counterpoint. The apparent resolution is severed by the household scene. Rhythm carries the Las Vegas-to-New York journey, rehearsal language, “SECOND READ,” and the finale.
2 AFTER THE APPLAUSE — Lena and Zay A close, 76 BPM soul/jazz duet (56 bars, approximately 2:57 of sung music). They discover mutual pleasure in practice and in being heard. The accompaniment loses bass, inner harmony, then pulse as Zay’s insult breaks the encounter. A brief instrumental fragment after his specific apology is deliberately left unresolved; it does not certify forgiveness.
3 TERMS AND CONDITIONS — Ben, Dani, Zay; ensemble fragments A funny, rhythmically exact negotiation of shelter, shifts, promises, and space. Offbeat domestic percussion grows from kettle, keys, and a folded bed. Ben’s automatic yes keeps entering before the question ends. Its count-and-set motif supports load-in and the final practical handoff.
4 WEIGHT OF MY OWN — Lena, Morgan Lena stops a composition that dictates her breath and authors a new relationship between movement and music. A measured ballet count bends into grounded R&B syncopation. Returns inside “HOLD FOR EIGHT” with Morgan following Lena’s chosen duration.
5 A ROOM THAT HOLDS — Velvet, Jude, Lena A live-act rehearsal becomes a negotiation over whose attention belongs where. Funk, theatrical vamp, and a guitar flourish are interrupted until the vocal cue leads. Velvet’s smaller paid show uses the revised arrangement in Act II, briefly and without adding a seventeenth full number.
6 WHAT THE LIGHT KEEPS — Iris, Zay The portrait sitting moves from heroic pose to reciprocal seeing. Suspended jazz harmony, pencil rhythm, and a melody whose final note changes when Iris discloses something about herself. An instrumental turn accompanies the finished mural; no triumphant portrait anthem.
7 COUNTERMELODY — Morgan, Jude A beautiful collaboration contains an avoided ownership argument. Morgan’s composed line and Jude’s guitar theme compete, then overlap without agreement. Its unresolved cadence is answered in “PUT MY NAME ON IT.”
8 IN THE FRAME — all eight Act I finale. Public praise and private objections collide around Rise of Reed. The opening’s wants reappear as material being edited into Zay’s story. Dense counterpoint remains intelligible through alternating focus. Fragmented phrases open Act II, stripped of the promo’s polish.
9 LOOK AGAIN — all eight in separate spaces Each decides what to do about the breach. Sparse piano, dry percussion, and exposed individual lines replace the promotional swell. Zay’s decision to remove the film lands before the ensemble rejoins. A short reflective phrase returns when he reviews game film honestly.
10 NO PUNCHLINE — Dani, with Ben present Dani keeps trying to make an admission entertaining. Comic rhythmic setups progressively fail; the music stops for the plain apology. A brief sung coda belongs to Dani alone, without Ben providing absolution. No reprise: the refusal to recycle the moment protects its sincerity.
11 PUT MY NAME ON IT — Morgan and Jude They name authorship, performance, payment, and limits. A clear melody replaces competitive overlays; Jude leaves rests. Morgan claims the musical phrase and the professional sentence. The score delivery uses a brief instrumental resolution of this theme.
12 HOLD FOR EIGHT — Lena, Velvet, Morgan; Zay later Rehearsal turns a fixed phrase into a shared, teachable score. Choreography counts become sung agreements. Sensuality and humor remain present; boundaries make the work more playable. Its taught handoff is used at the premiere by the substitute performer.
13 SECOND READ — Zay, Vale, court ensemble Zay receives a correction, repeats a rotation, and sees the pass. Percussion follows basketball work; held-ball passages carry the vocal peaks. The rising-fourth motif resolves downward rather than straining higher. Ray’s old practice count can recur instrumentally beneath Vale’s new instruction, connecting mentors without making either the author of Zay’s success. The camp climax uses the rhythmic idea without duplicating the entire song.
14 THE WORK OF STAYING — Ben, Dani, Iris; brief ensemble responses Ben asks for terms and tells the truth early. A steady, warm soul pulse carries schedules and practical labor without making them emotionally small. Dani’s career news does not erase the apartment conversation. A restrained instrumental tag marks the company’s chair stacking.
15 ENOUGH FOR TONIGHT — ensemble across Buffalo and New York Scrimmage and premiere unfold in parallel. Musical phrases answer across space while the events remain separate. The peak is a passed ball and a held count; neither event solves every career. Its final unresolved harmony leads through the epilogue rather than straight to applause.
16 BOUNCE (LEAVE SOME ROOM) — all eight The opening returns around 96 BPM, with rests now structurally necessary. Anyone can carry the pulse. Zay sings, listens, catches, passes. Distinct colors remain; the last beat can be human breath rather than a giant orchestral hit. Final reprise; a brief exit groove may continue the pulse without supplying a new dramatic ending.

Character motif transformations: Zay’s rising fourth softens into a playable response; Lena’s counted preparation acquires a self-chosen rest; Dani’s pickup enters later, after listening; Velvet’s held crown note becomes a shared harmony; Ben’s repeated low note gains a stable bass beneath it; Jude’s ornate turn becomes a plain offered phrase; Iris’s suspended second finds an honest, imperfect resolution; Morgan’s connecting figure finally receives a complete solo statement. Silence remains available to every character, especially where performance would evade responsibility.

sections.title: Complete opening sequence
sections.html:
7. Complete opening sequence

BOUNCE

Working stage text and lyric draft. Music and choreography are specified for development, rather than represented as a completed orchestral score.

Performance frame

August. Las Vegas, then New York City. The principals are adults. ISAIAH “ZAY” REED is twenty-six and six feet eight inches tall, a Las Vegas native who has worked and saved to pursue his New York Knicks dream. The opening is a symbolic overture across distance: eight lives occupy a shared theatrical space before most have met. Zay’s literal home scene is in Las Vegas; the other seven live in New York. No exchanged glance establishes acquaintance. The journey after the household scene must clearly mark an overnight flight and the next evening’s New York arrival.

DENISE, Zay’s mother, is a server at Las Vegas’s fictional Desert Star cabaret and lives with alcohol addiction. RAY “UNCLE RAY” WALKER, her former husband, is not a blood uncle. Denise’s partners were routinely introduced to Zay as “Uncle”; Ray continued coaching and mentoring him after the divorce. Supporting actors or a clearly identified offstage voice may play the family roles. They are not additional chakra principals.

The stage contains eight practical working stations at its perimeter. A court-sized central lane and two crossing diagonals remain clear. BEN has a taped audition mark and phone. LENA has a portable barre. DANI has a microphone. VELVET has a coat stand and mirror. JUDE has an amplifier and guitar. IRIS has an upright working panel. MORGAN has a keyboard, manuscript, and pencil. ZAY owns the open floor. These are suggestions of places, not eight complete rooms.

Faces receive neutral front light. The distinct colored halos and side light are yellow for Zay, red for Ben, orange for Lena, blue for Dani, violet for Andre/Velvet, green for Jude, indigo for Iris, and pearl white for Morgan. The first seven draw on the familiar chakra palette. Soul Star, the pearl-white eighth identity, is this production's artistic extension. That information belongs in the program and design materials; nobody explains it in dialogue.

Sound, timing, and safety

The number is 144 bars of 4/4 at a grounded 96 BPM: approximately six minutes, allowing a few seconds for the opening breath. No accelerando. The feeling of acceleration comes from subdivision and overlapping voices. The final cadence is interrupted during bar 144.

Amplify the actual basketball with boundary microphones at the court surface, with enough isolation to prevent footfalls from becoming false ball attacks. Zay uses a playable, properly inflated ball. The drummer watches Zay and matches the first audible impact with a low kick; performer and drummer rehearse a shared visible downward cue. The ball does not follow a prerecorded bounce track. The musical director holds the opening pulse and adjusts within the groove if a bounce travels. The click, if used, supports the band and never makes the actor chase it.

The marked lanes are dry, free of cables, and checked before every performance. Guitar leads run away from them. Nobody crosses a dribble lane without the rehearsed visual cue. Movement can be adapted to the actor's basketball skill without changing Isaiah's intelligence or pleasure. No blind throw toward another performer or the audience is necessary.

The repeating ball cell is two grounded attacks, a rest, then a quicker return. The useful action is the rest: Zay catches on it to sing sustained phrases. The same cell will later pass to feet, hands, guitar, and breath. Ball impacts are a musical voice, not continuous noise underneath every lyric.

Bars 1–8 · 0:00–0:20 · Ball and kick

BLACKOUT.

A breath. A shoe settles on wood.

A concentrated YELLOW SPOTLIGHT rises on ZAY, entering with a basketball at his hip. He surveys the space like a defender he intends to fool. A little smile: he likes this part.

He drops his weight.

His first dribble hits the floor precisely with a low KICK DRUM.

He catches the return. Lets the silence hang. Another impact and kick. He tests the distance to the edge of his light, crosses over, returns. A sharp, economical change of direction earns him a laugh he does not ask for.

For the last two bars he establishes the ball cell. The kick answers rather than doubles every impact. He catches at his sternum on the final rest.

Bars 9–24 · 0:20–1:00 · Zay's solo

A round bass note enters. Zay sings with the ball held; then resumes dribbling between phrases. His confidence is attractive and real, even if it is not secure.

ZAY

They painted over half the key.
I know the missing line.
The rim leans left. I lean right back.
This crooked court is mine.

Give me a hand that's closing fast,
Give me a second look.
You think you know which way I move—
You haven't read the book.

He sells a drive, plants, and slips sideways. A rim is unnecessary: the joy is in the choice, not a spectacular shot.

ZAY

Down to the floor—
Up to my hand.
A little more sky
Than they thought I could stand.

Don't hang my name up yet.
Leave room for what I do.
Give me the ball.
Give me a lane.
Give me a way through.

On “through,” he catches, looks up, and allows the bass to finish the thought.

Bars 25–32 · 1:00–1:20 · Ben, red

A RED HALO reveals BEN at his audition mark. Soft rim percussion enters. He presses record, assumes a genial face, dislikes it, and starts again.

BEN (spoken in rhythm)

Ben Mercer. Six— No. They can see how tall I am.

(He resets his own shoulders.)

Hi. I'm Ben Mercer.

BEN

Give me a room with a door that shuts,
A name on the chair by the wall.
One part I don't have to borrow—
Let me be there when you call.

Zay travels outside Ben's station on the upstage lane, never through his audition frame. Ben's final “call” remains audible after his red light settles.

Bars 33–40 · 1:20–1:40 · Lena, orange

An ORANGE HALO reveals LENA at the barre. Brushed shaker joins. She executes an exact ballet phrase, checks a position in an absent teacher's mirror, then catches herself doing it. She removes her hand from the barre. The next phrase uses the same balance with a grounded hip, an audacious pause, and a teasing glance at the audience. Neither vocabulary is presented as the correction of the other. Both belong to her.

LENA

Eight to get there, four to stay,
One to change my mind.
I can finish where you pointed—
I can leave that mark behind.

Zay's lateral slide and Lena's traveling step share a rhythm on opposite diagonals. They do not touch. Lena decides when her phrase ends.

Bars 41–48 · 1:40–2:00 · Dani, blue

A BLUE HALO reveals DANI, testing a microphone. The cable stays in its station. A clipped keyboard chord answers the ball.

DANI (spoken)

My family says I make everything a joke. Which is unfair. Some things are invoices.

There is a beat in which Dani almost says something else. The smile gets there first.

DANI

Give me seven paid minutes,
Give me people who stay.
If I tell it right, the terrible part
Can buy the train home today.

Zay pauses his dribble for the punchline. Then he continues through the cleared center as Dani tries a second microphone height.

Bars 49–56 · 2:00–2:20 · Velvet, violet

A VIOLET HALO finds ANDRE halfway into VELVET SAINT's final sleeve. Velvet completes the transformation in full view: an exact adjustment of the cuff, a check of the hem, then a walk that changes the scale of the room. Organ and handclaps arrive.

VELVET (to an imagined technician)

The special follows me, darling. I don't follow the special.

VELVET

Put my name above the doorway.
Leave my changes in the chart.
You can buy a seat this evening—
You don't get to buy the part.

Zay stops at the edge of Velvet's lane, gives the entrance its space, and rolls into a retreat dribble when the lane clears. It is a choreographic joke, not yet a relationship.

Bars 57–64 · 2:20–2:40 · Jude, green

A GREEN HALO. JUDE plugs into a waiting amplifier. His live lead guitar gives a distinctive phrase: a bent note that seems to resolve, two quick descending notes, then an unexpectedly open sustained tone. The band leaves the gap around it intact.

JUDE

Hear that note against the wire?
That's the one I came to find.
Let the room forget my fingers.
Let the sound stay in your mind.

He cannot quite resist embellishing the last measure. Zay slips behind him, safely outside the cable zone. Jude's riff becomes a counterline rather than a constant solo.

Bars 65–72 · 2:40–3:00 · Iris, indigo

An INDIGO HALO. IRIS is painting on the upright panel. She lifts an immaculate little reproduction away from her working surface, studies the image underneath, and makes one broad, irreversible stroke. A mallet voice enters, dry and resonant. The brush is visible; its contact is not artificially amplified.

IRIS

Somebody moved the window.
Everybody likes the view.
I remember where the light fell.
I can paint that shadow, too.

Zay crosses in front of the panel at a safe distance. She sees the interruption of light, chooses it, and adds another stroke. He does not yet know she exists.

Bars 73–80 · 3:00–3:20 · Morgan, pearl white

A PEARL-WHITE HALO reveals MORGAN. Morgan listens, pencils a rhythm, shifts an orchestral voicing at the keyboard, then removes one note. The removal allows Iris's last syllable and Jude's sustained guitar tone to meet. The first full harmony appears.

MORGAN

There's a place beneath your ending.
There's a word above that chord.
I can hear the song between us—
Let me put my name aboard.

Morgan starts to erase “my,” then sets the pencil down without erasing it. Zay dribbles around the station's outside edge and returns to center.

Bars 81–96 · 3:20–4:00 · Eight working bodies

The groove opens into funk. No new lyric begins in the first four bars: all eight actions can be seen. Zay works a retreat, crossover, and forward drive; Lena answers with a change of level; Ben resets an entrance; Dani adjusts the microphone; Velvet snaps the cuff; Jude mutes a string; Iris lifts and commits; Morgan marks a beat. These gestures share weight transfer and timing without pretending they are interchangeable skills.

Across the next twelve bars, entries occur two bars apart. Keep each new voice forward in the mix.

BEN

Give me a room—

LENA

Give me the count—

DANI

Give me a minute—

VELVET

Give me the whole amount—

JUDE

Give me a reason—

IRIS

Give me the wall—

MORGAN

Give me the credit—

ZAY (catching the ball)

Give me the ball.

It lands as a joke and an admission. He spins the ball once in his hands, pleased with the rhyme.

Bars 97–120 · 4:00–5:00 · Chorus

Full ensemble harmony, with soul warmth and gospel-rooted call and response. No generic wordless choir conceals an individual line. Zay sings the first call with the ball caught; the drummer carries its pulse. He resumes dribbling only during responses.

ZAY

What do you do when the floor comes up?

ALL

Bounce.

LENA / BEN

Find your feet. Take a breath. Get your weight back down.

ALL

Bounce.

DANI / VELVET

We have worked all week for a little of this town.

JUDE / IRIS / MORGAN

Let the window shake. Let the late train run.
There's a light still on where the work gets done.

ALL

Bounce—
Off the wood, through the wire,
Through the blister and the rent.
We can tell you what it costs us.
We can't tell you what we're worth yet.

Eight bars of dancing carry the last line's discomfort rather than resolving it. Zay's pathway threads between the stations in a figure eight, each crossing released by a visible shift of weight. A demanding vocal pickup comes only after he catches the ball.

ZAY

Put me where the light can find me.

ALL

Let it find us working here.

Bars 121–136 · 5:00–5:40 · Competing wants

The original short wants recur in an eight-part round, one entry every two bars. Ben's room, Lena's changing mind, Dani's paid minutes, Velvet's name, Jude's note, Iris's shadow, and Morgan's credit remain distinguishable. At first each tries to extend a phrase over the next. Morgan's hand draws the entries into a workable shape, but Morgan loses the end of their own line in doing so.

Zay returns to the central lane. The ball drives the whole room for four bars. He enjoys the power too much. His rhythm grows busier; other phrases have to squeeze around it. Lena finishes her own count anyway. Jude holds the open note instead of racing him. The room briefly finds balance by necessity.

ZAY

Hear me coming. Hear me coming.
There is more of me than this.

OTHERS, individually becoming an ensemble

There is more of me than this.

Bars 137–144 · 5:40–6:00 · Almost arrival

The harmony lifts without a key change. Eight colors remain distinct. Zay takes the ball down the final lane, catches it on bar 141, and plants to sing. The other seven turn toward their own imagined futures, never toward him as a savior.

ALL

Every fall has a rhythm.
Every hand can learn the ground.
If the world won't make a little room—
We will make a little—

HARD CUT.

No final chord. No button. No held tableau inviting applause.

The household

The seven other lights disappear. The band is silent. A harsh overhead practical reveals a cramped Las Vegas apartment kitchen. A location cue reads LAS VEGAS — AUGUST and is gone. A bill lies beneath a supermarket magnet; a saucepan soaks in a sink too small for it. DENISE REED stands in work trousers with one shoe off, her DESERT STAR server’s apron slung over a chair. Beside a folded order pad are a glass and a partly concealed bottle. They are ordinary evidence, not a comic prop or a diagnosis delivered by lighting. Zay's caught ball is at his chest. The symbolic space has collapsed around his actual body.

DENISE

“YOU NEVER GIVE ANYTHING TO THIS HOUSEHOLD WHO THE FUCK DO YOU THINK YOU ARE? YOU THINK YOU ARE A BASKETBALL STAR? BRING SOME MONEY INTO THIS HOUSE”

Zay's fingers tighten on the seams. His jaw contracts. His shoulders move inward by perhaps an inch. At six feet eight, he has learned exactly how little room he is allowed to occupy.

The clock on the microwave changes. Nobody moves.

DENISE

I called you.

ZAY

My phone was in the locker.

DENISE

Of course it was.

She takes a folded notice from beneath the magnet and puts it on the table. It is real. She does not have to wave it.

DENISE

They're charging another late fee. I asked for more hours. Desert Star cut Friday.

Zay looks at the total. He puts the ball on a chair; it rolls toward the edge and he catches it before it falls. Even that little sound would be too much.

ZAY

I put a hundred and twenty in the account Tuesday.

DENISE

And how far did that get us?

ZAY

I've got forty-seven on me. The flight's paid for.

DENISE

Then change it.

ZAY

It's tonight.

DENISE

And the money you've been hiding?

ZAY

Tryout fee. A room deposit. I told you.

DENISE

You always put that first.

He starts a reply, then swallows it. She sees the swallow and hears defiance.

DENISE

Don't stand there looking down at me.

He lowers his eyes. The adjustment is immediate, practiced, devastating.

ZAY

I'm looking at the bill.

Denise sits. She presses a thumb into the arch of her bare foot. Without thinking, she folds a table napkin one-handed into a neat fan; work is still in her fingers. Then she pushes the glass behind the order pad. Her exhaustion and her skill are visible. Neither undoes what she has said.

DENISE

You said last month would be different.

ZAY

I know.

DENISE

I can't spend “different.”

He takes his wallet out. Counts thirty dollars onto the table. Keeps seventeen. Denise looks at the division.

DENISE

So you do have money.

The old argument is ready to begin another circuit. Zay recognizes the route. He picks up the ball instead.

From a hook behind the door he takes a small, worn bag packed for the journey: training clothes, an old Knicks cap, a thin document folder. He adds his charger and a clean pair of socks from the drying rack. The fare and tryout budget are in a separate account built from years of shifts; the forty-seven dollars is the cash in his wallet, not all his money. He has no confirmed bed in New York. There is no triumphant music. Packing is clumsy with the ball under his arm.

DENISE

What are you doing?

ZAY

Going out.

DENISE

Where?

He has no answer. He checks his pocket for keys twice.

DENISE

Fine. Walk away. You're good at that.

He stops at the door. The audience can see the speech he could make. He does not make it.

He opens the door. He leaves.

The door closes with an ordinary, imperfect latch. Denise remains at the table for one breath before her light goes out.

sections.title: Complete transition and bar scene
sections.html:
8. Complete transition and bar scene

The journey to The Switch

KEYS. LATCH. FOOTSTEPS.

Zay stands outside the door, motionless. Through it, a chair scrapes. He starts walking before he can turn back.

The stairwell appears through two cold practicals. His bag knocks the handrail. He switches shoulders. A downstairs television sounds through a wall; a recorded laugh ends before he reaches it. He has to duck at the last flight's low pipe. His height is inconvenience now, not power.

At the building’s exit, a key strikes another key. Las Vegas traffic fills the space: service vehicles and the hiss of a bus, with distant entertainment spilling from a doorway. Zay’s steps settle into a slower version of the opening cell. A percussionist finds the keys’ small metallic interval, then stops when he stops at the crossing. The city does not obey him.

He wakes his phone. A prepaid flight confirmation is briefly legible: LAS VEGAS → NEW YORK. Beneath it, a separate note lists tryout fee, transit, food, room deposit. Saving enough to go has not made him safe when he arrives.

He calls UNCLE RAY.

RAY (on the phone)

You outside?

ZAY

Yeah.

RAY

Same corner. Five minutes.

A pause. Ray hears the breathing he has heard after bad practices and worse nights.

ZAY

She says you put this in my head.

RAY

You had a Knicks jersey before I had a key.

Zay almost smiles. Ray does not make that into a victory over Denise.

ZAY

You going back there?

RAY

No. I can take you to the airport. I'm not going back into that marriage.

Zay looks at the building. Ray allows the silence.

RAY

Still want the ride?

ZAY

Yeah.

RAY

All right. You got the whole game on that drive? Not just the buckets?

ZAY

Even the ugly ones.

RAY

Those are the ones a coach can use.

Two headlights open a narrow path. Ray enters only far enough to take the bag; he asks with a hand before Zay gives it over. A car door closes. The keys’ rhythm becomes an indicator click. Their goodbye can be played with two chairs, avoiding a realistic vehicle.

RAY

Dani know you're coming?

ZAY

Knows I'm landing. Doesn't know I'm asking for a floor.

RAY

Ask before you make it somebody else's plan.

Zay nods, not yet able to do it. Ray offers his fist. Zay meets it.

RAY

Wednesday. Send me the film if you want me to look.

The offer has a day and a task. It is not a promise to fix everything. Zay takes the bag. Ray’s light goes out as an airport announcement rises.

OVERNIGHT FLIGHT. A brief location-and-time cue reads NEW YORK — THE NEXT DAY. The hiss of cabin air becomes train brakes. The ball stays contained at Zay’s feet; no dribbling through an airport or transit car. A moving band of daylight crosses him, then evening streetlight. The audience must not mistake the journey for a walk between two neighborhoods.

Outside a New York station, he wakes his phone and types to DANI: You still at Switch?

Three dots. Then: Second set at ten. Side door. Don't heckle. I'm fragile and insured badly.

Zay almost laughs. He types Can I— and deletes it. He puts the phone away without asking for somewhere to sleep. Ray’s practical advice has not instantly changed him.

A bass note grows from the departing train. Brushes borrow his walking pulse. The music remains underscoring, with no new song. Zay arrives at THE SWITCH, a New York neighborhood bar and cabaret with a small raised stage, a proper rehearsal floor, and a back corridor shared with its dressing area. This is not the Desert Star where Denise works in Las Vegas. Dani is Zay’s childhood friend from Vegas, now building a career here.

Its noticeboard distinguishes separate bookings: comedy tonight, dance on another night, a live-music night, and Velvet's coming drag show. The place supports overlapping working lives; it does not stage every art form simultaneously.

Dani is finishing a set. Zay slips through the side entrance and stands where Dani can see him.

DANI (to the room)

My roommate bought a label maker. Now the milk says BEN. Which feels less like a boundary and more like we're drinking evidence.

Laughter.

DANI

You've been very kind. Please tip the people doing the work you can't interrupt with a microphone.

Applause. Dani steps offstage, clocks the bag, and lets the smile relax.

DANI

All the way from Vegas, and you brought luggage to my set. Finally, an honest review.

Zay gives half a smile.

DANI

Bad?

ZAY

Can I just be here a minute?

DANI

Yes.

Dani nearly adds a joke. Doesn't.

DANI

I've got ten minutes to argue about the money I already agreed to. Water's free. Put the ball under your chair, NBA.

ZAY

Not NBA.

DANI

I know. Neighborhood Basketball Acquaintance.

That gets him. Dani heads toward the manager. A bar worker gives Zay water after his small requesting gesture. He puts the bag between his feet and wedges the basketball beneath his chair.

LENA enters from the back corridor in street clothes, carrying a dance bag and a rolled rehearsal mat. She has returned for equipment after sharing an earlier rehearsal slot with Velvet. She is not performing tonight. She checks a note on the next dance-night schedule, makes a correction with her own pen, and notices Zay trying to fit both knees beneath a tiny table.

LENA

That one hates tall people. Take this one.

She indicates a table with a central pedestal, then sets her mat beside it. She is choosing to stay, not being assigned to tend him.

ZAY

You know the furniture personally?

LENA

We work together. Some of it's difficult.

He moves. She sits opposite, leaving him an easy way out of the conversation.

LENA

You always turn your foot before you sit down?

ZAY

Do I?

LENA

Little pivot. Like the chair's going to steal something.

ZAY

You always watch people's feet?

LENA

Better than watching their mouths. Feet usually tell you first.

He deliberately squares his feet. She laughs.

ZAY

Now I can't sit naturally for the rest of my life.

LENA

Sorry. Occupational hazard.

ZAY

You dance?

LENA

I do. Here some nights. Other rooms. Currently in a room with a radiator that only understands tropical weather.

ZAY

I play. Currently in a gym where the shower only understands winter.

LENA

We could exchange complaints. Balance the climate.

He shifts the basketball with his heel, then catches himself.

LENA

Don't stop. I like watching somebody do a thing they don't have to think about.

ZAY

That's the part you think about the most. So you don't have to.

She recognizes something precise. A moment of genuine attention.
