LENA

Yes.

At the piano, the interval musician touches a soft chord while settling for the next set. A yellow side light finds Zay; orange warms Lena's side of the table. Faces remain natural. The room's normal activity recedes without disappearing. Neither is suddenly on the cabaret stage.

AFTER THE APPLAUSE

An intimate original duet. 4/4, approximately 76 BPM, 56 bars: just under three minutes. The opening ball cell appears in brushed percussion, with the last attack omitted. Piano or Rhodes carries the harmony; a restrained bass and occasional guitar harmonic leave air around the singers. The ball stays under the chair throughout.

Bars 1–8 · Lena

Lena tries the melody as if telling a story to one person. There is wit in the first line, then an unprotected detail.

LENA

Someone always wants a picture
Just before I take my shoes off.
Hold it there. A little longer.
Let the camera have its proof.

They can keep the perfect angle.
I would like my little chair.
Half an orange in a paper bag,
And someone glad I'm there.

Bars 9–16 · Zay

Zay picks up her final interval, a crooner's quiet answer. He is surprised to discover he can sing softly and still be heard.

ZAY

Someone always has a question
When I'm waiting for the train:
How's the weather? Can you dunk it?
Say the height and guess the name.

I can reach the highest cupboard.
I can lift what you can't move.
Sometimes I would like a question
With nothing left to prove.

Bars 17–24 · First chorus

LENA

After the applause,

ZAY

After all that sound,

BOTH

Could we leave the bright part standing
While the rest of us sits down?

You don't have to name the future.
You don't have to fix the night.

LENA

Just move your glass—

He moves it out of the space she wants for her forearm.

ZAY

There's room.

BOTH

This much is all right.

Bars 25–32 · A game of practice

Their fingers mark a small pattern on the table, almost the opening rhythm. Lena changes the final accent. Zay listens before answering.

ZAY

First you plant—

LENA

Then you listen—

ZAY

Then you make the other move.

LENA

That's your game. In mine, I get to
Pick the thing I'm moving to.

ZAY

Fair correction.

LENA

Try it slower.

BOTH

Let the empty beat go by.

They do. For a full bar neither fills the space. Their enjoyment needs no kiss to be legible.

Bars 33–40 · The cost of being seen

LENA

I like the eyes. I like the entrance.
I like knowing what I know.
I just want to choose the moment
When I'm finished with the show.

ZAY

I like winning. I like flying.
I like making people stand.
When my feet come back beneath me,
Could I still deserve a hand?

Bars 41–56 · Shared chorus and quiet landing

BOTH

After the applause,
After all that sound,
Could we leave the bright part standing
While the rest of us sits down?

Let the ice give up its edges.
Let the last train shake the light.
There's a place across this table.
You can stay a little while.

The last eight bars stretch the final exchange into space for thought.

LENA

No picture.

ZAY

No score.

LENA

Just a little—

ZAY

Little more.

BOTH

After the applause.

The cadence is modest and complete. Beneath the following conversation, the pianist begins a quiet, unmetered variation. This is not another verse. It will come apart in response to what they say.

The duet breaks

ZAY

You learned all that here?

LENA

Some. Ballet first. Years of it. Then other things. The best floorwork teacher I ever had could open a beer with her shoe. Terrible trick. Incredible teacher.

ZAY

You still do ballet?

LENA

When I can get the room. I'm trying to make something that doesn't have to explain which kind of dancing it is before it starts.

ZAY

I'd watch that.

She accepts the compliment. Then he continues, intending generosity.

ISAIAH

“You’re too good for this place. You could be a real dancer again.”

The piano fails to complete its returning figure. Lena's hand stops on the table.

LENA

“Again?”

ISAIAH

“I mean, you could do something with your talent.”

LENA

“I just paid my rent with my talent.”

ISAIAH

“That’s not what I meant.”

LENA

“Then tell me what you meant.”

The bass leaves. The pianist keeps a single open interval, quietly, waiting for him as she is waiting.

ZAY

I mean a company. A proper stage. Where people come for the dancing.

LENA

What do you think people come for when I dance?

ZAY

You know what I mean.

LENA

I am giving you the chance to say it.

He looks toward the stage, then at the poster advertising a dance night. For the first time he notices what he had been able to ignore while enjoying her.

ZAY

It's just—if people see you like that, they don't see what else you can do.

LENA

You sat here for ten minutes. What did you see?

He cannot answer quickly enough.

LENA

Was I doing fine until you worked out where the money came from?

ZAY

No. I respect the work. You've got to do what you've got to do.

The open interval collapses to one note. Lena leans back, the physical opposite of their earlier shared space.

LENA

You keep telling me you respect it while you find another way to say I should be ashamed of it.

ZAY

I'm saying you deserve better.

LENA

Better pay? Better conditions? A floor that doesn't wreck my knees? Yes. The people who pay me being embarrassed to admit what I do? You brought that part with you.

Silence. The pianist takes both hands off the keys. The room has ordinary sound again: ice, a till, someone laughing too loudly at the far end.

ZAY

Look, I had a bad night. I was trying to say something good.

LENA

And now I have to help you feel good about saying it?

He catches his jaw tightening, the same gesture from home. He does not yet understand the repetition. The audience can.

ZAY

That's not fair.

LENA

No. It isn't.

She stands, takes the mat, and moves it out of his reach. It is a work tool, not a barricade. She lowers her voice before she raises it.

LENA

I want this conversation finished. Leave.

He begins to stand, but the need to repair his own image outruns his ability to listen.

ZAY

If you'd just let me explain—

LENA

“GET OUT. GET THE FUCK OUT!”

The room stops. She does not need to repeat herself. The bar worker opens a clear path to the side door. Dani, returning, sees Lena's face and does not make a joke or ask her to lower her voice.

Zay retrieves his ball and bag without touching her, reaching around her, or asking for one more minute. He leaves immediately. Nobody applauds Lena. Nobody plays a comic sting. She is shaking with anger, and angry about having to shake.

At the door, Zay almost looks back. He keeps going.

Outside, the city sounds larger than before. He stands with the basketball pressed against his hip. For a moment, habit suggests a dribble. He lowers his hand, but catches the ball before he releases it.

No kick drum comes to meet him.

END OF SEQUENCE.

9. Visual brief and standalone image-generation prompts

Identity and key art

BOUNCE. EVERY FALL HAS A RHYTHM.

Build the title as B + basketball + UNCE. The basketball replaces the only O; it is never an extra illustration above an otherwise complete word. Its visible diameter matches the cap height of B, U, N, C and E, with recognizable black seam lines. Use heavy, condensed lettering with open counters. Keep seams strong enough to survive a thumbnail. Test the mark in one color and at 160 pixels wide. The web wordmark is live type with the same photorealistic leather 3D ball in every logo, keeping spelling reliable.

The core world is charcoal, worn court timber, nighttime pavement and the warm orange of a working ball. Yellow isolates Isaiah. The other seven identities stay visible as their own colors: Lena orange, Dani blue, Andre/Velvet violet, Ben red, Jude green, Iris indigo, Morgan pearl white. Faces need neutral fill; colored lighting must not make people unreadable. The seven-chakra palette is a design foundation. BOUNCE's pearl-white Soul Star is a theatrical extension, not a statement that this full eight-part arrangement is a universal traditional system.

Isaiah belongs at the center of the key art, with his body grounded and the ball in his possession. Give the artists evidence of work: a rehearsal floor, an amplifier, a microphone, an unfinished painting, marked score pages, an audition script and drag costume construction. They are people pursuing their own work, not an admiring chorus around a savior. Preserve separate zones within a shared city. Avoid generic championship trophies, literal mystical diagrams, floating inspirational words, fake reviews and invented production credits.

The current website uses original generated concept art, not actual cast photography. It depicts a possible ensemble and environment. A production photoshoot would replace it once performers and designers are attached. The website poster is a composition study; final print key art should be generated or photographed specifically for a 2:3 crop so all seven supporting figures survive.

Loading sequence

A dark field. The whole BOUNCE wordmark is already legible, with the ball occupying the O's allotted width. The O dribbles continuously in its allotted column until the progress reaches 100%. Each cycle models a downward hand push, a gravity-driven fall, a floor rebound and the next hand contact. The world-space trajectory is scaled to the logo’s available headroom. Strong continuous backspin follows a fixed oblique axis with contact damping; it does not reverse with the bounce. At 100%, the final flight and short settling contacts finish. The letter positions remain still. The ball carries an original Bounce athletic-script wordmark with a normal letter o, plus an original vertical navy-and-orange badge of Zay dunking. These replace manufacturer and league marks. This on-ball wordmark is distinct from the main BOUNCE title, whose O remains the ball. A complete CC0 basketball mesh preserves the wrapped leather texture, normal detail and dark seam channels. The ink wraps around the same surface and rotates with it. The final settling turn presents both marks upright toward the viewer; the share image and still fallback use that same pose. Letter shadows fall consistently from an upper-left light; the ball’s separate floor shadow tightens and darkens at contact and softens at height. Behind the logo, a wireframe continental United States carries a small animated flight from Las Vegas to NEW YORK CITY, with the destination label to the right of the coastline. The aircraft, traveled route and visible loading percentage advance from the same progress value. At 100%, the map dissolves into an original dark-navy architectural blueprint of MSG: fine ivory lines describe the circular arena’s elevation, facade grid and roof, with an overhead seating plan and central basketball court below. The user’s blueprint reference sets the visual character; no retail frame or branding is reproduced. Hold this arrival image briefly, then open the pitch. The ball settles at the shared baseline, then the ensemble artwork appears. The reference is the economy and comic timing of a theatrical studio ident, expressed through an original basketball action. No lamp, borrowed lettering or copied choreography.

Allow a skip button immediately, a replay control later and a reduced-motion version with a stationary ball. A transparent Blender render of the same custom-branded model remains available as a fallback if 3D rendering is unavailable. All navigation, hero, poster and footer marks use the same ball, with traveling orange highlights on the actual seam channels as well as the outside rim. After loading, each completes a full three-dimensional turn in approximately five seconds on a varied axis and makes occasional small vertical hops at different times. These stop off-screen, when motion is paused, and under reduced-motion settings. A clean 1200×630 shot of the resting loading logo is the social share image. Titles, subtitles and all clickable labels are uppercase; paragraphs are justified throughout. The sequence is a short presentation animation, not a claim that assets are still downloading. Sound is off by default. An optional separate rhythm sketch demonstrates 96 BPM and is explicitly labeled as a sketch, not a cast recording or finished song.

Film language

Match the ball's drop to a heel lowering from relevé; match its return to Jude's hand coming off a string. A brush wipes across a painted face; a rehearsal mirror gives way to a cramped home window. The opening's color worlds intercut separate locations and do not imply that the eight have already met. Hold on Zay long enough to enjoy him before broadening the ensemble.

The cut to Denise’s Las Vegas home has no dissolving glow or emotional underscoring. Carry the journey through keys, a door, Uncle Ray’s car, an overnight flight and New York transit; the next evening’s bar encounter must never imply the cities are adjacent. A ball caught at chest height becomes a held breath. At The Switch, orange and yellow can coexist without blending into a new symbolic identity. During the insult, ordinary room light gradually becomes more legible as the song loses its shelter. In the climax, use match cuts and musical counterpoint across the Buffalo camp and New York premiere, preserving travel geography. The finale connects their lives without falsely putting all eight in the same place at once.

Standalone image-generation prompt: logo

Create an original, immediately legible theatrical wordmark reading exactly “BOUNCE”, spelled B–O–U–N–C–E. Replace the letter O entirely with one round basketball. There must be no separate typographic O behind or beside the ball. Use heavy condensed sans-serif uppercase letters, warm off-white, on a flat near-black theatrical background. The basketball is a highly photorealistic orange-brown pebbled leather ball with familiar deep, dark rubber seam channels, matching a professional regulation basketball. Print an original Bounce wordmark in bold connected athletic script with an ordinary letter o on the leather, above an original vertical navy-and-orange badge of the fictional protagonist leaping to dunk. No manufacturer or league logos. Keep this small on-ball lettering distinct from the main title. Its visible diameter equals the visible cap height of the surrounding letters and it sits on their baseline. Tight, deliberate optical spacing. The result must read BOUNCE instantly at both poster scale and 160-pixel thumbnail size. One title only. Proportionate orange neon around every letter and the basketball rim and seams; no extra balls, no additional headlines, no sports-team badge, no lamp, no borrowed studio logo. Crisp typographic lettering paired with a photographic leather ball and consistent upper-left lighting. Leave sufficient quiet margin around the complete mark.

Standalone image-generation prompt: theatrical poster

Create a premium original 2:3 vertical theatrical poster for an adult contemporary New York ensemble musical and feature film titled exactly “BOUNCE”. At the top, a bold, immediately legible condensed uppercase wordmark in warm off-white: B + an orange basketball replacing the O + UNCE. The basketball must have recognizable black seams, match the cap height of the letters and occupy the O's actual place. Do not add a second O. At the bottom, set exactly “EVERY FALL HAS A RHYTHM.” No other text, review quotes, awards or billing.

Center Isaiah “Zay” Reed, a fictional Black male basketball hopeful, age 26, 6'8”, in ordinary worn practice clothing with an orange basketball. He is athletic, playful and human, not superheroic. A concentrated yellow overhead light gives him a readable face and grounded presence. Around him, show exactly seven other adult principals in distinct, legible environmental zones: Lena, a ballet-trained exotic dancer authoring a sensual, disciplined rehearsal phrase in orange; Dani, a comedian working a microphone in blue; Andre as the commanding drag performer Velvet Saint in violet; Ben, an actor rehearsing a marked script in red; Jude, a lead guitarist working at an amplifier in green; Iris, a painter making an unfinished portrait in indigo; Morgan, a composer with keyboard and handwritten score pages in pearl white. Each is absorbed in their own work rather than gazing at Isaiah. All eight figures must remain inside the final crop.

Use dark theatrical space grounded in a real nighttime New York court and neighborhood workrooms, tactile pavement and timber, fine cinematic grain, rich charcoal shadows and restrained basketball-orange details. Maintain eight distinct pools of light with neutral face fill, never a generalized rainbow haze. Leave breathing room for the exact title and tagline. Emotional tone: funny, sensual, bruised and hopeful. Avoid mystical chakra symbols, fantasy powers, halos shaped as religious icons, championship trophies, celebrity likenesses, additional people, extra basketballs and watermarks. Original concept casting only.

Ball material prompts used for the loading animation

Leather texture, based on the supplied reference: Extract the reference’s warm orange-brown pebbled basketball leather into a flat seamless square PBR albedo texture, uniform diffuse illumination, dense fine pebbles, no sphere, no black seams, no letters, numbers, logos or marks.

Transparent fallback, based on the supplied reference: Create a single photorealistic basketball cutout from the reference, preserving realistic orange-brown pebbled leather, spherical geometry and curved recessed black channels. Remove all text and branding, restoring matching leather. Center the full ball on transparency with soft studio light from upper left, no floor or external cast shadow.

Neon and arena presentation update

Each BOUNCE wordmark retains its readable light letterforms and gains a proportionate orange neon contour. A brighter segment travels around the actual Anton glyph outline; the realistic leather O has matching light traveling around its rim and along its recessed seam lines, all aligned with its rotation and bounce. The loading scene reveals a dark-navy architectural blueprint of Madison Square Garden after the flight reaches New York City at 100%. Scene-photo edges dissolve into the dark page through gradient masks. Motion can be paused and is reduced for visitors who request reduced motion.

The arrival artwork is an original vector architectural illustration inspired by the supplied blueprint reference. The continental-U.S. outline uses public-domain Natural Earth data. The interface identifies the arrival drawing as a concept elevation and schematic plan. No venue endorsement is claimed.

Reading interaction

The site begins a gentle automatic scroll three seconds after the hero is revealed, at a 45% setting corresponding to 45 pixels per second. A visitor’s wheel, touch, pointer or keyboard interaction pauses it; an explicit Resume control restores it. Reduced-motion preferences prevent automatic start. The score stays click-to-expand, with a white plus/minus indicator.

Interactive character portraits

Every person in the uncropped hero ensemble is a keyboard- and touch-accessible profile target. Hover or keyboard focus illuminates the figure in their character color. Selecting a figure opens a translucent dark window with their concept portrait, ambition, conflict, and progress, drawn from the same character data as EIGHT COLORS. WHOLE PEOPLE. Escape, the close control, or the surrounding backdrop closes the window and restores focus. The large story background is textured basketball orange; yellow remains Zay’s small character and lighting accent.

songs.title: BOUNCE
songs.purpose: Six-minute opening. Ball and kick establish a 96 BPM groove; bass, percussion, harmony, guitar, and keys enter in layers. Each principal gets an audible want before counterpoint. The apparent resolution is severed by the household scene.
songs.music: Reprise: Rhythm carries the Las Vegas-to-New York journey, rehearsal language, “SECOND READ,” and the finale.

songs.title: AFTER THE APPLAUSE
songs.purpose: A close, 76 BPM soul/jazz duet (56 bars, approximately 2:57 of sung music). They discover mutual pleasure in practice and in being heard. The accompaniment loses bass, inner harmony, then pulse as Zay’s insult breaks the encounter.
songs.music: Reprise: A brief instrumental fragment after his specific apology is deliberately left unresolved; it does not certify forgiveness.

songs.title: TERMS AND CONDITIONS
songs.purpose: A funny, rhythmically exact negotiation of shelter, shifts, promises, and space. Offbeat domestic percussion grows from kettle, keys, and a folded bed. Ben’s automatic yes keeps entering before the question ends.
songs.music: Reprise: Its count-and-set motif supports load-in and the final practical handoff.

songs.title: WEIGHT OF MY OWN
songs.purpose: Lena stops a composition that dictates her breath and authors a new relationship between movement and music. A measured ballet count bends into grounded R&B syncopation.
songs.music: Reprise: Returns inside “HOLD FOR EIGHT” with Morgan following Lena’s chosen duration.

songs.title: A ROOM THAT HOLDS
songs.purpose: A live-act rehearsal becomes a negotiation over whose attention belongs where. Funk, theatrical vamp, and a guitar flourish are interrupted until the vocal cue leads.
songs.music: Reprise: Velvet’s smaller paid show uses the revised arrangement in Act II, briefly and without adding a seventeenth full number.

songs.title: WHAT THE LIGHT KEEPS
songs.purpose: The portrait sitting moves from heroic pose to reciprocal seeing. Suspended jazz harmony, pencil rhythm, and a melody whose final note changes when Iris discloses something about herself.
songs.music: Reprise: An instrumental turn accompanies the finished mural; no triumphant portrait anthem.

songs.title: COUNTERMELODY
songs.purpose: A beautiful collaboration contains an avoided ownership argument. Morgan’s composed line and Jude’s guitar theme compete, then overlap without agreement.
songs.music: Reprise: Its unresolved cadence is answered in “PUT MY NAME ON IT.”

songs.title: IN THE FRAME
songs.purpose: Act I finale. Public praise and private objections collide around *Rise of Reed*. The opening’s wants reappear as material being edited into Zay’s story. Dense counterpoint remains intelligible through alternating focus.
songs.music: Reprise: Fragmented phrases open Act II, stripped of the promo’s polish.

songs.title: LOOK AGAIN
songs.purpose: Each decides what to do about the breach. Sparse piano, dry percussion, and exposed individual lines replace the promotional swell. Zay’s decision to remove the film lands before the ensemble rejoins.
songs.music: Reprise: A short reflective phrase returns when he reviews game film honestly.

songs.title: NO PUNCHLINE
songs.purpose: Dani keeps trying to make an admission entertaining. Comic rhythmic setups progressively fail; the music stops for the plain apology. A brief sung coda belongs to Dani alone, without Ben providing absolution.
songs.music: Reprise: No reprise: the refusal to recycle the moment protects its sincerity.

songs.title: PUT MY NAME ON IT
songs.purpose: They name authorship, performance, payment, and limits. A clear melody replaces competitive overlays; Jude leaves rests. Morgan claims the musical phrase and the professional sentence.
songs.music: Reprise: The score delivery uses a brief instrumental resolution of this theme.

songs.title: HOLD FOR EIGHT
songs.purpose: Rehearsal turns a fixed phrase into a shared, teachable score. Choreography counts become sung agreements. Sensuality and humor remain present; boundaries make the work more playable.
songs.music: Reprise: Its taught handoff is used at the premiere by the substitute performer.

songs.title: SECOND READ
songs.purpose: Zay receives a correction, repeats a rotation, and sees the pass. Percussion follows basketball work; held-ball passages carry the vocal peaks. The rising-fourth motif resolves downward rather than straining higher. Ray’s old practice count can recur instrumentally beneath Vale’s new instruction, connecting mentors without making either the author of Zay’s success.
songs.music: Reprise: The camp climax uses the rhythmic idea without duplicating the entire song.

songs.title: THE WORK OF STAYING
songs.singers: Ben, Dani, Iris; brief ensemble responses
songs.purpose: Ben asks for terms and tells the truth early. A steady, warm soul pulse carries schedules and practical labor without making them emotionally small. Dani’s career news does not erase the apartment conversation.
songs.music: Reprise: A restrained instrumental tag marks the company’s chair stacking.

songs.title: ENOUGH FOR TONIGHT
songs.singers: ensemble across Buffalo and New York
songs.purpose: Scrimmage and premiere unfold in parallel. Musical phrases answer across space while the events remain separate. The peak is a passed ball and a held count; neither event solves every career.
songs.music: Reprise: Its final unresolved harmony leads through the epilogue rather than straight to applause.

songs.title: BOUNCE (LEAVE SOME ROOM)
songs.purpose: The opening returns around 96 BPM, with rests now structurally necessary. Anyone can carry the pulse. Zay sings, listens, catches, passes. Distinct colors remain; the last beat can be human breath rather than a giant orchestral hit.
songs.music: Reprise: Final reprise; a brief exit groove may continue the pulse without supplying a new dramatic ending.
